title: The Hungry Huskies Win It All
dek: A year after an academic ban kept them out of the NCAA tournament, seventh-seeded UConn never trailed Kentucky's freshmen and won its fourth national title, 60-54.

setup.text: In April 2012 the NCAA turned down UConn's final appeal: because of the program's past Academic Progress Rate scores, the Huskies would be barred from the 2013 postseason. UConn's president complained that current players were paying for the grades of students no longer enrolled. That September, with Jim Calhoun retiring, Kevin Ollie — a former UConn point guard with a 13-year NBA career and two years as an assistant — was named head coach.

The fallout was heavy. Three players transferred and two left for the NBA, and when the Big East broke apart UConn landed in the new American Athletic Conference. Shabazz Napier, a freshman on the 2011 title team, stuck around. So did Ryan Boatright.

The 2013-14 Huskies started 9-0, then wobbled. In January, between road losses at Houston and SMU, Ollie took them on a tour of AT&T Stadium and told them to picture coming back in April. They closed the regular season 24-7 — the finale a 33-point loss at Louisville on March 8 — and, after losing the AAC tournament final, entered the NCAA tournament as the No. 7 seed in the East.

Then they ran: No. 10 Saint Joseph's in overtime, No. 2 Villanova, No. 3 Iowa State, No. 4 Michigan State, and No. 1 overall seed Florida, 63-53, in the semifinals. Kentucky — the preseason No. 1, seeded eighth in the Midwest with five freshmen in its starting lineup — had won its previous three games on late shots by Aaron Harrison.

story.text: UConn came out sharp: Boatright scored eight of UConn's first 19 points, and the Huskies led 30-15 with 5:59 left in the half. At one point in the half, with UConn struggling to solve Kentucky's zone, Napier hit a 3 from about 30 feet, at the edge of the Final Four logo at center court. In a luxury box, former Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush watched side by side.
Kentucky would not go away. The Wildcats closed the half on a 16-5 run to trail 35-31, and Aaron Harrison's 3 twelve seconds into the second half made it 35-34.

UConn pushed the lead back to 48-39 with 11:01 left. Then James Young dunked over freshman center Amida Brimah for a three-point play, starting an 8-0 Kentucky run. In the middle of it Boatright twisted his left ankle; he called timeout, had it worked on and came back. Young's two free throws with 8:13 left made it 48-47.
Kentucky's misses at the line hurt: the Wildcats made 13 of 24 free throws, while UConn made all 10 of its attempts.

sequence.text: Young makes two free throws. Kentucky is within a point.
Aaron Harrison, Kentucky's big-moment shooter, fires from the left corner for the lead. It misses, and Lasan Kromah rebounds.
Napier answers with a well-guarded 3 just before the shot clock expires.
Napier finds Niels Giffey, and Giffey's 3 makes it a five-point game.
Randle makes one of two free throws.
Boatright, playing on the bad ankle, hits a step-back jumper.
Alex Poythress dunks a Randle miss, then misses the free throw.
DeAndre Daniels scores inside, credited to a Napier assist.
Kromah goes to the line with 25.1 seconds left and makes both. UConn is 10 for 10 from the line.

quotes.text: You're looking at the hungry Huskies
quotes.role: UConn senior guard, Final Four Most Outstanding Player

quotes.text: When you ban us, and it's not our fault? We were hungry. I wanted to introduce everybody to the hungry Huskies.
Yeah, somebody told me we were Cinderellas. And I was like, No, we're UConn. I mean, this is what we do.
Because they're not missing. Those guards never miss.
quotes.role: Kentucky head coach, on why Kentucky did not foul late

aftermath.text: Napier knelt and pressed his forehead to the court after the buzzer, and he was wiping away tears when he cut down the net. He finished with 22 points, six rebounds and three assists and was named the Final Four's Most Outstanding Player; Boatright and Daniels joined him on the all-tournament team.

The next night in Nashville, UConn's unbeaten women beat Notre Dame 79-58 for their ninth title, making UConn the only school to win the men's and women's championships in the same year twice — the first time was 2004.
On April 8 Gov. Dannel P. Malloy greeted the champions at Bradley International Airport, and on June 9 President Barack Obama honored the UConn men's and women's champions at the White House.

legacy.text: UConn was the first No. 7 seed ever to win the title, and the first champion since Arizona in 1997 without a conference regular-season or tournament crown.

Ollie became the first coach since Michigan's Steve Fisher in 1989 to win a national title within two years of taking his first Division I head job, and joined John Thompson, Nolan Richardson and Tubby Smith as Black coaches who led Division I teams to the title.
Napier, Giffey and Tyler Olander, seniors who had also been on the 2011 champions, became the first UConn players with two national titles.
